title: South Sea Directors Convert the National Debt Into Bubbled Equity, Bribe Parliament, and Crash a Nation

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The South Sea Company charged holders of government annuities steep conversion premiums to swap solid debt for its own shares, skimming the spread between par and the inflated market price on every exchange.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The June 1720 Bubble Act outlawed rival joint-stock promotion, legislating a speculation monopoly for a company that simultaneously bribed ministers and MPs with ledger-entered stock, as the 1721 Commons inquiry documented.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Insider knowledge of the conversion terms and bribes circulated through the subscription ledger while the public was fed visions of Spanish South American trade windfalls the company could not legally deliver at scale.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Directors, ministers, and well-placed subscribers sold into a tenfold 1720 price rise ahead of the September crash, capturing windfalls from stock issued against debt the state still had to service.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Walpole's resolution — known as the Screen — restored the tainted elite rather than prosecuting it, and his management of the cover propelled him into lasting control of the government by 1721-1722.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The 1694 Bank-of-England settlement of public debt onto a chartered monopoly was weaponized: the South Sea Company replicated the debt-conversion model with equity instead of banknotes.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Bubble Act and the 1721 inquiry established the template for a captured regulator-lawmaker complex — Parliament criminalizing rivals while laundering its own members' corruption through a managed inquiry.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Recovered or preserved fortunes, Walpole's included, flowed back into Whig financing and ministerial patronage, converting scandal into the working capital of a generation-long oligarchy.
closedLoopRatchet.enablesNextDossier: The Screen demonstrated that systemic fraud could be resolved by elite self-pardon, a precedent that shaped every subsequent receivership, whitewash inquiry, and managed collapse from the 1720s forward.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: The pop-culture image of a nation gone mad for bubbles — deluded small investors ruined by their own greed — reduces the affair to crowd mania.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commons inquiry's stock ledger entries showed the operation was engineered from within: bribery of ministers and MPs, a Bubble Act written to concentrate the mania, and insiders selling before the crash.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The chartered entity and its 1807-1820 winding-up Acts survive in the corporate lineage record; the 1721 Commons inquiry records document the bribery mechanics; the 1719-1720 conversion scheme's tenfold rise and September 1720 crash are established chronology.
